sourceTopic: Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass

history.title: Check Before You Claim

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Bubbles are not proof. Neither is a colour change. This week you learn what actually counts as evidence that a new substance formed, and why mass that seems to disappear never really does.

1. Read **Did Anything New Actually Form?**
2. Learn the words in **Reaction Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Study the **Signs and Their Impostors** chart — it is the heart of the unit.
4. Trace **What Happens to the Atoms** before the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Chemical or Physical?**
6. Take **Reaction Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Two Rules**.
8. Read **Reaction Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Investigation: Account for the Atoms**.

Your job this week: catch one claim — an advert, a video, a classmate — that treats a sign as if it were proof. ⚗️

Picture panels: Identity and rearrangement; Clues need context; Everyday reaction examples; New solids and conserved atoms. Text-free illustrations use editable captions and image-specific descriptions. Diagrams simplify scale, anatomy and processes; colors and tokens are explained in captions. Follow the lesson text for scientific context. Educator review is pending.

history.title: Did Anything New Actually Form?
history.data:
## Did Anything New Actually Form?

A liquid fizzes. Did a reaction happen? Perhaps. Bubbles can also come from boiling or gas escaping from a drink. They show that gas is present, but not where it came from.

A chemical **reaction** forms new substances. Atoms rearrange and bonds change. **Reactants** are used in the change; **products** form. Some reactant may be left over. Some product may already be in the starting mixture.

A pure **substance** has a set chemical makeup. Its **properties**, such as density, help us study it. Conditions matter: the same material can have different density at a different temperature. A mixture can also behave differently from a pure substance.

In a **physical** change, the chemical identity stays the same. Boiling water is still water. When ordinary sugar dissolves in water, its molecules spread out but remain sugar. Getting the sugar back supports that account. Yet “can it be reversed?” is not a sure test. Some chemical reactions can go in both directions too.

Useful **indicators** include bubbles, color change, a change in temperature, light, and a solid appearing. A **precipitate** is a solid that separates from a solution. A reaction can form a new solid that does not dissolve.

Look for other explanations as well. Adding water can make a colored solution paler. Some physical mixing can warm or cool materials. A hot object may glow. Particles already in a liquid can settle. Crystals may appear as water leaves, without a new substance forming.

Use several observations and suitable tests. Compare materials under matched conditions. Does the evidence identify a new substance? Could temperature, concentration or an impurity explain the difference instead?

Now track the matter. When wood burns, it combines with oxygen from the air. Gases and ash form. We cannot compare only the wood and ash: that leaves out the oxygen that came in and gases that left.

In an ordinary chemical reaction, **atoms** of each element are **conserved**. They are not created or lost. In a closed system, no matter enters or leaves. Its mass stays the same at the precision of classroom tools. Count the same apparatus and all materials before and after. Check for leaks and measurement error if results differ.

Our colored tokens model atoms. The red and blue pairs are an invented counting example, not a real reaction or a recipe. The drawn boxes mark system boundaries, not containers to seal and heat. Use the model to ask where every atom went.

Impostor: water boiling, or dissolved gas escaping
Ask: is the gas a new substance?

Impostor: dilution, or two colours simply mixing

data.title: Remember the Two Rules
data.instructions: Two cards hold the reasoning. Study the example, build one of your own, then explain what it keeps you from getting wrong.
data.sourceExcerpt: Indicators need context. Identify substances under matched conditions, then account for all atoms and all material crossing the system boundary.

cards.target: An indicator is a prompt to investigate, not proof
essentialFacts: The five indicators are bubbles, colour change, temperature change, light, and a precipitate.
Every one of them has a physical impostor.
Use several appropriate tests under matched conditions and rule out physical explanations.
cards.aiExample: CLUE, CHECK, ACCOUNT: notice a clue, check chemical identity under matched conditions, then account for atoms. A clue begins an explanation; it does not finish one.
cards.mapping: The cue links an observation with alternative explanations and a test; it does not turn one changed property into proof.
cards.scaffoldStarter: The clue is ____. Another explanation is ____. My controlled test is ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick one of the five indicators.
Say what would actually settle it.
coachPrompts: What conditions would need to stay the same in your comparison?
cards.studentPrompt: Build your own phrase for what an indicator is worth.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why is treating a sign as proof the most common mistake here?

cards.target: Why mass is conserved even when it looks lost
essentialFacts: Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction; they are rearranged.
Wood burning takes in oxygen and releases gases; weighing only ash misses both.
A closed system conserves mass at classroom precision; compare the same complete system.
cards.aiExample: Think of a bag of alphabet tiles. Rearranged into new words, the tiles are the same tiles and the bag weighs the same. Tip some on the floor and it only looks lighter because you stopped counting those.
cards.mapping: Tiles cannot be created by spelling, which is exactly the constraint atoms are under, and the tiles on the floor stand in for the gases nobody weighed.
cards.scaffoldStarter: The atoms are like ____. When mass looks lost, really ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick something that can be rearranged but not created.
Say what it does not change.
coachPrompts: In the burning log, what are the tiles on the floor?

history.title: Reaction Check

questions.question: A beaker of clear liquid starts bubbling. What have you established?
options: That a chemical reaction is definitely taking place
That a gas is being produced by new substances
That the liquid must have been an acid to begin with
Gas is present; its source still needs investigation
questions.correctAnswer: Gas is present; its source still needs investigation

questions.question: Which observation would best settle whether a reaction occurred?
options: The mixture became warmer while it was being stirred
Tests identify a new substance and rule out physical causes
The color shifted from dark blue to a paler shade of blue
Bubbles rose from the bottom as the liquid was heated
questions.correctAnswer: Tests identify a new substance and rule out physical causes

questions.question: Why is sugar dissolving in water a physical change?
options: Sugar molecules remain sugar while spreading through water
Because no bubbles or colour change happen while stirring
Because water is a liquid and sugar is a solid substance
Because the mixture does not get hot enough to react
questions.correctAnswer: Sugar molecules remain sugar while spreading through water

questions.question: Burning a log leaves ash weighing far less than the wood. Why is mass still conserved?
options: Some mass converts into the heat and light given off
Mass is only conserved in reactions that stay sealed
The comparison omits incoming oxygen and outgoing gases
The ash is denser, so the balance reading misleads you
questions.correctAnswer: The comparison omits incoming oxygen and outgoing gases

questions.question: What actually happens to atoms during a chemical reaction?
options: Some are destroyed and replaced by different atoms
They are rearranged into different groupings, none lost
They are compressed, which is why products weigh less
New atoms form from the energy released by the change
questions.correctAnswer: They are rearranged into different groupings, none lost

questions.question: A classmate mixes two liquids, sees the beaker get warm, and writes "a chemical reaction occurred." What is wrong with that reasoning, and what should they check?
questions.expectedAnswer: Temperature change has multiple possible causes. Physical mixing or some dissolving can change temperature, while other dissolving involves reactions. Compare identified materials under matched conditions, using multiple tests and checking temperature, concentration and purity before concluding that a new substance formed.

questions.question: A teacher supplies data for a gas-forming reaction in open and closed systems. What must you compare to test conservation of mass?
questions.expectedAnswer: Compare the same complete system before and after, including apparatus, all reactants and all products. In the closed-system data the gas remains within the measured boundary, so the mass difference should be consistent with measurement uncertainty. In the open system some gas leaves that boundary. Analyze supplied data; do not seal a gas-producing reaction in a rigid container.

history.title: Reaction Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Is cooking a chemical change? 🍳
data.answer: Cooking can cause both kinds of change. Browning makes new substances. Melting changes state. Being hard to reverse does not, by itself, tell us which kind occurred.

data.question: Does mass conservation hold in nuclear reactions?
data.answer: Nuclear changes need an account of both mass and energy. The tiny mass changes linked to energy transfers in ordinary chemistry are too small for classroom tools to detect. Nuclear changes can also change one element into another.

data.question: Why does a cut apple go brown? 🍎
data.answer: Cutting damages cells. Oxygen, enzymes and other materials can then take part in browning reactions. Color alone would not identify a reaction in an unknown material.

data.question: Can a reaction go backwards?
data.answer: Many reactions can run both ways. At equilibrium, the two directions proceed at the same rate. The amounts stay steady even though reactions continue.

data.question: Is dissolving really not a reaction? 🧂
data.answer: It depends on the materials. Sugar molecules stay sugar when they dissolve in water. Other materials can react as they dissolve. Check what substances are present.

data.question: How did anyone prove atoms are conserved before they could see one?
data.answer: They made careful mass measurements while tracking matter that entered or left. A balanced equation also accounts for each kind of atom. Small measurement differences need to be checked against the limits of the tools.

data.title: Account for the Atoms
data.instructions: Analyze teacher-supplied mass data for a gas-forming reaction in open and closed systems. Build a particle model and explain any apparent mass change. This is a data investigation, not an instruction to run a sealed reaction.
data.fitReason: Students model conservation and evaluate system boundaries and measurement uncertainty using supplied observations.

brief.context: Use these invented practice measurements for a reaction and its apparatus: open system, 152.40 g before and 151.96 g after; closed system, 152.40 g before and 152.39 g after. The estimated uncertainty of each mass difference is ±0.03 g. Assume gas is the only matter leaving the open system. These are teaching data, not experimental results collected by this class.
brief.audience: A group in the year below who have been told mass is conserved and do not believe it
brief.drivingQuestion: Which mass differences are consistent with the stated uncertainty, and how do the system boundaries explain them?
brief.seedDirection: Draw each system boundary and list all material and apparatus included. Subtract before from after, then compare the size of each difference with ±0.03 g.
lockedLessonFacts: Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction; they are rearranged.
An open system can exchange matter, including gases, with its surroundings.
Mass is conserved for a closed system at classroom precision.
An indicator such as bubbling is a prompt to investigate, not proof.
openQuestions: What exactly has to be on the balance for the measurement to be fair?
Is each difference larger than the supplied uncertainty?
How would a leak affect a nominally closed system?
stakeholders: The younger group who need convincing
Your partner, who checks the calculations
Anyone reviewing your interpretation of the supplied data
criteria: Copy all four supplied masses and identify both system boundaries
Calculate both differences with units and show the subtraction
Compare each difference with the stated uncertainty, not just the number of decimal places
The explanation accounts for the open result without abandoning conservation
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: Use supplied data and paper or digital particle tokens only
Do not heat or seal gas-producing mixtures; no chemical procedure is part of this activity
No claim without a measurement behind it
brief.deliverable: A one-page report with two system sketches, a table of supplied masses and calculated differences, a particle model, and an explanation of the open result. Label all supplied values as invented practice data.

parallelExample.context: In a separate invented example, a closed-system difference is -0.02 g with estimated difference uncertainty ±0.04 g.
parallelExample.move: The group treats that difference as consistent with zero within uncertainty. It does not claim that the result proves exact equality or that the instrument resolution alone defines uncertainty.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: A measurement is interpreted with its uncertainty and system boundary, rather than treating every nonzero digit as a physical loss.

supports.frameStarter: The open-system difference is ____ g; the closed-system difference is ____ g. Compared with ±0.03 g, ____.
frameChoices: Draw the open and closed boundaries
Build an atom-token model with equal atom counts
Explain a hypothetical leak using the same boundary
coachPrompts: Was everything that ended up on the balance also on it at the start?
Is your difference bigger than your balance can actually resolve?
Could you convince someone who does not already believe you?

data.coachHint: Expected differences: -0.44 g and -0.01 g. The latter is consistent with zero within ±0.03 g; account for escaped gas in the open system.
data.sourceExcerpt: Count all matter inside a defined boundary and evaluate differences against measurement uncertainty.
